text: This section is the canonical, code-grounded description of every product module that ships inside CoLab. It exists so that any engineer, architect, product manager, or operator joining the project in the next five years can understand *what* each module does, *why* it exists, *how a user touches it*, *how a request actually travels through the stack*, and *what it depends on* — without reading nine thousand lines of `CoLabV1.tsx` first.

CoLab is a single-page collaboration suite — chat, calls, meetings, tasks, reminders, files, and more — delivered as one Next.js client application talking to one Express API, one MySQL database, one Socket.IO realtime plane, and a LiveKit media plane for audio/video. The entire frontend is *one* client-rendered SPA mounted at `/`; there are no nested routes. In-app navigation is **state-driven, not URL-driven**: a single `mode` string in the god-component `CoLabV1.tsx` decides which view renders. Understanding that one fact unlocks the rest of the architecture.

title: How to read this section
text: Every module below follows the same five-facet template — Purpose, User Flow, Business Value, Technical Flow, Dependencies — so you can jump to any module and find the same shape of answer. Where a module is only partially built or not built at all, that is stated plainly under Purpose and repeated under Technical Flow. Nothing here is aspirational; every claim is grounded in files that exist in the repository today.

Before the per-module detail, here is the shape of the whole system. Five planes cooperate: the **client SPA**, the **REST API**, the **realtime plane**, the **media plane**, and **persistent storage** (MySQL plus S3-compatible object storage). Most modules use the first three; only Calls, Meetings, Screen Sharing, and Recording reach into the media plane; only Files and Recordings reach into object storage.

text: A few cross-cutting truths apply to *every* module and are not repeated under each one:

items: **No global URL routing.** The whole app lives at `/`. Navigation is the `mode` state string in `CoLabV1.tsx` (switch at ~line 4206). A view is a React component, not a page.

**No Redux/Zustand/Jotai.** State is centralized in `CoLabV1.tsx` via dozens of `useState` plus `useRef` mirrors (`tokenRef`, `messagesByConvRef`, `socketRef`, `conversationsRef`, etc.) so callbacks always read the latest value. Props are drilled into child views; `ChatView` is `React.memo`'d for performance.

**Same-origin everything.** The browser talks only to its own origin. Next.js rewrites proxy `/api/*` and `/socket.io/*` to the backend and `/livekit/*` to the SFU, so attachments, sockets, and signalling all share one origin and one TLS cert.
**One envelope contract.** Every REST response is `{ok, data, error}`; non-ok throws an `Error` with `err.status` attached, and callers key off `403` for access-denied reasons (call/meeting gates).

**Auth is a single JWT.** A 7-day HS256 token (`clb_token` in `localStorage`) authenticates every REST call (Bearer header) and the socket handshake (`auth.token`). There is no refresh token; on expiry the user re-authenticates.

text: Authentication establishes *who a user is* and issues the credential that gates every other module. It is fully shipped and enterprise-grade: server-side credential policy, constant-time password verification, audit logging of every auth event, and token revocation on logout. It is the trust root of the product — nothing else works without it.

items: User lands on the SPA; `CoLabV1` restores any `clb_token` from `localStorage` and calls `api.me()` to validate it.
If there is no valid token, `LoginScreen.tsx` renders. The user enters email + password and submits Login (or Signup, if the signup feature flag is on).
On success the backend returns a JWT; the client stores it, sets `me`, initializes E2EE (a no-op when E2EE is off), connects the socket, and switches `mode` to `dashboard`.
A signup additionally opens the first-run `Onboarding.tsx` wizard.
Logout calls `POST /api/auth/logout`, which blocklists the token, and the client clears local state.

text: Authentication is the gate that makes a multi-user workspace possible and keeps it compliant. The credential policy (length, character classes, disposable-domain blocking, common-password rejection) reduces account-takeover risk; the audit trail satisfies governance and incident-response requirements; token revocation means a logout (or account deletion) actually ends a session rather than leaving a live bearer token in the wild.

**Frontend:** `LoginScreen.tsx` calls `api.login`/`api.signup`. **Backend:** `routes/auth.ts` exposes `POST /signup`, `POST /login`, `GET /me`, `POST /logout`, `DELETE /account`. `authService.ts` hashes passwords with Node's built-in `scrypt`, storing `saltHex:hashHex`, and verifies with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (constant-time). `credentialPolicy.ts` validates email and password server-side *before* account creation — the client mirror in `lib/passwordPolicy.ts` is for live UX only and is not authoritative. JWTs are minted with HS256, payload `{sub:userId, name}`, TTL `AUTH_TOKEN_TTL` (default `7d`). **Middleware:** `middleware/auth.ts` reads `Authorization: Bearer`, verifies via `authService.verify`, then checks `tokenBlocklist.isBlocked` (Redis-backed, in-memory fallback). **DB:** the `users` table holds `email` (unique), `password_hash`, and `role`. **Realtime:** the socket handshake re-verifies the same JWT (but does *not* re-check the blocklist — only HTTP middleware does). Every auth event is written to `audit_log`.

title: Failure scenarios & troubleshooting
text: 401 on every authed request usually means an expired or blocklisted token — the frontend dispatches `colab:unauthorized` (after re-validating via `/api/auth/me` to avoid logout on transient blips) and logs the user out. A boot refusal in production means the prod secret guard rejected a default/weak `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` (<32 chars) — set a strong secret. If logout 'doesn't stick' on one instance after a Redis outage, the blocklist fell back to per-instance memory; confirm `REDIS_URL` and Redis health.

items: `users` table; `audit_log` (governance).
`tokenBlocklist` service (Redis or in-memory).
Every other module — they all require the JWT this module issues.
Settings/Onboarding for first-run; the socket plane for the post-login handshake.

text: The Dashboard is the default landing view after login — a data-driven overview that orients the user before they dive into a conversation. It is shipped. It has no dedicated route or table of its own; it aggregates data from existing APIs (frequent contacts, missed calls, upcoming meetings).

items: After authentication the app sets `mode='dashboard'` and the Dashboard renders as the landing screen.
The user sees at-a-glance panels: frequent people, recent/missed calls, and upcoming meetings.
Clicking a panel item navigates (state change) into the relevant module — e.g. a contact opens a DM, a meeting opens the meeting view.

text: A purpose-built landing screen reduces time-to-action: instead of dumping the user into a raw message list, it surfaces the few things that most likely need attention. It also showcases the breadth of the product on first impression, which matters for demos and adoption.

**Frontend:** `DashboardView` is defined *inline* inside `CoLabV1.tsx` (around line 5477) and rendered when `mode==='dashboard'` (branch ~line 4399). It reads already-fetched state (users, calls, meetings) held in `CoLabV1`, so it makes few or no extra calls. **Backend/DB:** none unique to the Dashboard — it reuses the `users`, `calls`, and `meetings` endpoints/tables. The body is tagged `mode-dashboard`, which is also the only context where the ambient Aurora-Borealis background (`body.amb-borealis.mode-dashboard`) is allowed to render.

items: Contacts/Users (frequent people).
Calls (missed/recent).
Meetings/Calendar (upcoming).
No dedicated backend route or table.

text: Messaging is the heart of CoLab: rich-text conversations across DMs, groups, and channels, with reactions, threads, editing, pinning, bookmarking, forwarding, scheduled send, read receipts, and optional DM end-to-end encryption. It is fully shipped and is the single most exercised code path in the product.

items: User selects a conversation in `ConversationSidebar.tsx`; `ChatView.tsx` renders the message list and composer.
They type in the TipTap-based `RichTextEditor`, optionally attach a file, record a voice note, @-mention, or reply to a message, then send (Enter; Shift+Enter inserts a block).
The message appears instantly (optimistic render) and is reconciled when the server echoes it back.
They can react with an emoji, edit, delete (for me / for everyone), pin, bookmark, forward to other conversations, or schedule a message for later.
Read receipts (ticks) update as peers read, subject to each user's receipt-privacy setting.

text: Messaging is the daily-use surface that justifies the product's existence — it replaces email threads and external chat tools with one governed, searchable, auditable workspace. Rich previews, threads, and scheduled send reduce noise and context-switching; the per-message and per-conversation controls (pin, bookmark, mute, star) let teams self-organize at scale.

**Frontend:** `ChatView.tsx` (~6,300 lines) owns the list, composer, reaction bars, and threads. All message *previews* (sidebar rows, reply quotes, forward cards) go through the single source `lib/messageText.ts` (`messagePreview`/`messageRowPreview`); only the bubble itself renders sanitized HTML (`lib/sanitizeHtml.ts`, DOMPurify). Sending normally goes over the socket (`MESSAGE_SEND`) for low latency, with REST endpoints as the durable fallback. **Backend:** `routes/conversations.ts` exposes the full surface — list/create conversations, `GET/POST /:id/messages` (keyset pagination via `?before&limit<=100`), edit/delete, `/react`, `/bookmark`, `/pin`, `/delete-me`, threads, scheduled messages, members, star/mute/hide/read. `services/messageService.ts` enforces an `assertMember` 403 gate and DM block enforcement. **DB:** `messages` stores rich HTML in `body`, attachments in `file_json`, reactions *inline* in `reactions_json` (there is no separate reactions table), threads via `parent_message_id`, plus `edited`, `forwarded`, `pinned`, and a `deleted` tombstone. A FULLTEXT index `idx_messages_fts` powers search. **Realtime:** on send, the server broadcasts `MESSAGE_NEW` to the conversation room — *that broadcast is the acknowledgement*; there is no separate per-message ACK event. Edits, reactions, pins, and soft-deletes ride `MESSAGE_UPDATED`.

steps.label: Broadcast MESSAGE_NEW
steps.detail: io.to(conv:<id>) — the echo IS the ack

steps.label: Client reconcile
steps.detail: replace optimistic by _clientId; bump preview; notify

title: Failure scenarios & troubleshooting
text: If a message never appears for the sender, the server may have emitted a sender-only `message:rate_limited` (token bucket exceeded) or `message:send_failed` (e.g. BLOCKED DM). If messages arrive only on refresh, the socket likely fell back to polling or lost its room — the client re-emits `CONVERSATION_JOIN` and refetches on reconnect. If a DM send is rejected, check `invites`/`user_blocks`: DMs are gated by an accepted connection and blocked-user enforcement.

items: Conversations/Members tables and services.
Realtime plane (delivery + typing + receipts).
Files/Attachments (per-message `file_json` and the Files module).
Reactions, Voice Messages, Notifications (mentions/replies), Search (FTS).
Optional E2EE (DM-only, off by default).

text: Calls provide ad-hoc audio/video between two people (1:1) or a whole conversation (group huddle) over the LiveKit SFU. The application code is fully shipped — signalling, token minting, host controls, screen share, voicemail, and 1:1-to-group promotion. The *media plane* (ICE/DTLS reaching the SFU/TURN across networks) is an infrastructure concern that must be verified per deployment; off-network calls require TLS, a reachable SFU public candidate, and a working TURN relay.

items: From a DM the user clicks the audio or video call button; the callee's app rings with Accept/Decline.
On accept, both clients mint a LiveKit room token and join the same room; media flows client → SFU → client.
In a group conversation, a huddle can be started; members are rung and can join; an owner/admin can mute-all or remove a participant.
Either party can toggle camera, mic, or screen share, or promote a 1:1 call to a group.
If unanswered, the call is logged as missed; a decline can carry a text reply that lands in the DM; an unanswered call can leave a voicemail.

text: Bringing real-time voice/video into the same workspace removes the friction of jumping to a separate conferencing tool and keeps call history, voicemail, and call-log pills in the conversation record. Group huddles enable spontaneous team sync; host controls keep larger calls orderly; the call-log and voicemail trail give an auditable record of who called whom.

**Frontend:** the 1:1/group call UI lives *inside* `CoLabV1.tsx` (the `CallModal` and incoming-ring), reusing the `.ms-*` CSS classes that also style the meeting UI — one styling source for both. `lib/callDiagnostics.ts` + `CallDebugPanel.tsx` give WebRTC observability (ICE/TURN candidate-pair, relay usage, RTT, loss). **Realtime signalling:** `realtime/socket.ts` handles `CALL_REQUEST/ACCEPT/DECLINE/CANCEL/HANGUP` with in-memory no-answer timers; group huddles use `HUDDLE_JOIN/LEAVE/SYNC/RING` backed by `huddleStore` (Redis when `REDIS_URL` set, in-process Map fallback). **Backend:** `routes/calls.ts` provides `GET /` (history), `POST /token` (mint LiveKit token, membership-gated), `POST /diag-token` (preflight probe room), group host controls (`mute-all`, per-participant mute/remove, owner/admin-gated), voicemail endpoints, and `POST /:callId/add-participants` (promote 1:1 → group). `services/livekitService.ts` mints the token (identity `userId__<uuid>` so an honest reload doesn't trip DUPLICATE_IDENTITY) and embeds `iceServers` (coturn) in the response. **DB:** the `calls` table records `kind`, `status`, `duration_sec`; it deliberately has *no* soft-delete trio. **Media:** LiveKit SFU on ports 7534 (signalling) / 7532-udp / 7531-tcp / 7533-udp (built-in TURN), with coturn as the external TURN relay (3478/5349/443).

title: The #1 deployment failure: media plane, not app code
text: "Calls fail / Unable to reach media server" over plain-HTTP bare IP is an insecure-context block (browsers refuse getUserMedia/wss without HTTPS) plus a `ws://localhost` LiveKit URL — fix with a TLS front and origin-derived `wss://host/livekit`. Cross-network calls that ring but never connect are an ICE/DTLS reachability problem (SFU public candidate or TURN unreachable), not application code. Use `CallDebugPanel` (`?calldebug=1`) to see whether a relay candidate was selected and whether TURN was even advertised.

items: LiveKit SFU + coturn TURN (media plane).
Realtime plane (signalling, huddle store, missed-call sweep).
Conversations/Members (membership gates the room token).
Voicemail service + `voicemails` table; Notifications (missed-call).
Screen Sharing (same code path).

text: Meetings are *scheduled* video sessions with a full conferencing UI: lobby/waiting room, lock, host and co-host controls, eject, hand-raise, in-meeting chat and reactions, join-by-ID/link, and Outlook-style recurrence. It is fully shipped on the application side. (Server-side recording is a separate, partially-deployed concern — see 2.24.)

items: A user schedules a meeting from the Calendar/Meetings view (title, start time, duration, optional recurrence); invite cards post into the relevant conversation.
At meeting time, invited users (or anyone with the meeting ID/link) open `PreJoinMeeting`, check devices, and join.
If a lobby is enabled or the meeting is locked, non-hosts wait until a host/co-host admits them.
Inside `MeetingStage`, participants see tiles, can raise a hand, send chat, react, and share screen.
The host can mute-all, mute/eject individuals, promote/demote co-hosts, toggle lobby, and lock the meeting; the meeting can be completed or cancelled.

text: Meetings turn CoLab into a self-contained video-conferencing platform, removing dependence on external tools and keeping scheduling, attendance, in-meeting chat, and (where enabled) recordings inside the governed workspace. Lobby, lock, and eject give hosts the control needed for sensitive or large meetings; recurrence supports standing ceremonies (standups, weeklies).

**Frontend:** `MeetingsView.tsx` (scheduling/list), `MeetingStage.tsx` (~2,850 lines — the full in-room UI), `MeetingRoom.tsx` (full-page wrapper), and `PreJoinMeeting.tsx` (device check). Meeting room options mirror the call options except `videoEncoding.maxBitrate` is 1.7 Mbps (vs 3 Mbps for 1:1). **Backend:** `routes/meetings.ts` covers scheduling (+recurrence, posts invite cards), invite, RSVP/leave, room lifecycle (`enter/heartbeat/leave`), cancel/complete, host controls (mute-all, per-participant mute/promote/demote/readmit, eject), lobby (toggle/list/admit/deny/admit-all), lock, and recordings. `services/meetingService.ts` enforces `enterRoom` (consults eject → lock → lobby, throwing 403 with reasons like 'ended'/'removed'/'locked'/'not admitted yet'); host gating is `requireMeetingHost`/`requireMeetingHostOrCoHost`. **DB:** `meetings` (+`lobby_enabled`, `locked`, `recurrence`, structured `recurrence_rule` from migration 0047), `meeting_attendees`, `meeting_lobby`, `meeting_presence`, `meeting_ejected` (persists across token re-mint), `meeting_messages` (persisted in-meeting chat), `meeting_recordings`. A DB trigger rejects scheduling meetings in the past. **Realtime:** `MEETING_JOIN` is access-gated by `canAccessMeeting` and replays the last 100 chat messages; `MEETING_CHAT_SEND`, `MEETING_HAND_RAISE/LOWER`, and `MEETING_REACTION` broadcast to the meeting room. **Media:** same LiveKit SFU as calls; the meeting UUID is the access credential, but the real gate is `enterRoom`.

steps.label: Join LiveKit room
steps.detail: meeting:<id> socket room; chat replay; tiles

steps.label: Host controls live
steps.detail: mute/eject/promote via RoomServiceClient by user-id prefix

title: Eject persistence
text: A host eject is durable: it is written to `meeting_ejected` and `enterRoom` consults it *first*, so a re-mint of the room token can't smuggle an ejected user back in. The ejection record is cleared when the meeting ends.

items: LiveKit SFU + coturn (media).
Realtime plane (join gate, chat, hands, reactions, presence).
Calendar (meetings are the calendar's data source).
Conversations (invite cards post as messages).
Recording service + `meeting_recordings` (optional, see 2.24).

text: Contacts is the people directory: browse colleagues, view profiles, start DMs/calls, and manage safety (block/report). It is shipped, including structured profile fields (title, pronouns, phone, timezone).

items: User opens Contacts from the Rail; `ContactsView.tsx` lists directory members.
They open a person to see profile details (title, pronouns, phone, timezone, about).
From there they start a DM or a call, or take a safety action: block or report.
Their own profile is edited via Settings/profile (`PATCH /api/users/me`).

text: A directory makes a workspace navigable as it grows — people can find and reach the right colleague without external lookups. Block/report gives users and admins a safety mechanism; structured profile fields (timezone especially) support distributed-team coordination.

**Frontend:** `ContactsView.tsx`. **Backend:** `routes/users.ts` — `GET /` (directory), `GET /frequent`, `PATCH /me` (profile), and safety: `GET /blocks`, `POST/DELETE /:id/block`, `POST /:id/report`, `GET /reports`. `services/blockService.ts` enforces blocks (which also gate DM sends). **DB:** `users` (with `title`/`pronouns`/`phone`/`timezone` from migration 0038), `user_blocks`, `user_reports` (both from migration 0031). **Realtime:** a profile/avatar/name/manual-presence change emits `USER_UPDATED` *globally* (one of the few `io.emit` broadcasts) so every client refreshes that user's chip.

items: Authentication/Users.
Messaging (start DM) and Calls (call a contact).
Block enforcement is consumed by Messaging and Direct Messages.

text: Calendar is a time-based *view* over scheduled meetings (and reminder due-dates). It is shipped. Critically, there is **no separate calendar table** — the calendar reads `meetings.starts_at` and `reminders.due_at`. In navigation, Meetings and Calendar share the same render branch.

items: User opens Calendar from the Rail (`mode==='calendar'` or `'meetings'` — same branch).
They see meetings laid out by date/time and can create a new meeting from the view.
Clicking an entry opens the meeting detail / join flow.

text: A calendar view turns a flat meeting list into a planning surface, helping users see their day/week and avoid conflicts — without the cost of building and syncing a separate calendar subsystem, because it is purely a projection of existing meeting and reminder data.

**Frontend:** `CalendarView.tsx`, rendered by `CoLabV1.tsx` when `mode==='calendar'||'meetings'` (branch ~line 4331). **Backend:** reuses `routes/meetings.ts`. **DB:** reuses the `meetings` table (`starts_at`, `duration_min`, `recurrence`); recurrence is expanded client/server-side from the structured rule. No calendar-specific endpoint or table exists.

items: Meetings (its entire data source for events).
Reminders (due-date overlay).

text: "Activity" is the in-app notifications feed — the nav label for the notifications module. It is shipped. It collects mentions, replies, missed calls, meeting invites/starts, file shares, and reactions into one read/unread feed, and drives the Rail badge.

items: A badge on the Rail 'Activity' item shows the unread count, pushed live over the socket.
User opens Activity; the feed lists recent notifications with type, actor, and target.
Clicking an item navigates to the source (message, call log, meeting).
Items can be marked read individually or all at once; the badge clears.

text: A unified activity feed ensures nothing important is missed across many conversations and modules, and gives a single place to triage — reducing the chance that a mention, missed call, or meeting invite slips through. The live badge keeps attention without requiring the user to poll each conversation.

**Frontend:** rendered inline in `CoLabV1.tsx` when `mode==='activity'` (branch ~line 4352); the Rail label 'Activity' maps to id `activity` with `notifUnread` as its badge. **Backend:** `routes/notifications.ts` — `GET /`, `/unread-count`, `POST /:id/read`, `/read-all`, `DELETE /:id`. `services/notificationService.ts` produces notifications from message mentions/replies, reactions, missed calls, and meeting invites. **DB:** `notifications` table (`type`, `title`, `actor_id`, `target_type/target_id`, `is_read`; migration 0028). **Realtime:** `NOTIFICATION_NEW` (full object to the recipient's user room), `NOTIFICATION_READ`, and `NOTIFICATION_COUNT` (the live badge number).

title: In-app only — no push
text: Notifications are delivered in-app and over the socket only. There is no web-push / browser-notification implementation; if the tab is closed, the user sees the count on next open rather than an OS notification.

items: Messaging (mentions/replies/reactions), Calls (missed), Meetings (invites/starts), Files (shared).
Realtime plane (live count + new-notification push).

text: Tasks is a native Kanban-style work-item board with status, priority, assignee, labels, due dates, dependencies, comments, and an activity log. It is shipped.

items: User opens Tasks; `TasksView.tsx` shows columns by status (todo/in-progress/done, etc.).
They create a task with title, assignee, priority, labels, and due date.
They drag a card to move its status, add comments, set dependencies, and watch the activity log.
Bulk operations are available for multi-task edits.

text: Built-in task tracking keeps work-item management inside the same tool as the conversations that spawn it, removing the round-trip to a separate project tool and keeping assignment, status, and discussion co-located. Dependencies and an append-only activity log support accountability and lightweight project governance.

**Frontend:** `TasksView.tsx` (`mode==='tasks'`), with a count badge in the Rail. **Backend:** `routes/tasks.ts` — CRUD plus `/bulk`, `/:id/move`, `/:id/deps`, `/:id/comments`, `/:id/activity`; `services/taskService.ts`. **DB:** `tasks` (status, priority, `assignee_id`, `labels` JSON, `project`), `task_activity` (append-only, no soft-delete), `task_comments`, `task_deps` (dependency graph). **Realtime:** a thin `TASK_CHANGED` empty signal is broadcast globally; the client responds by refetching tasks (a 'changed' signal, not a delta payload).

items: Authentication/Users (assignee/reporter).
Realtime plane (change signal → refetch).
Self-contained otherwise (own tables and service).

text: Reminders are personal to-dos with optional folders, due dates, priority, status, and recurrence. It is shipped. Reminder due-dates also feed the Calendar view.

items: User opens Reminders; `RemindersView.tsx` lists items, optionally grouped into folders.
They add a reminder with text, due date, priority, and recurrence; organize into folders.
They tick items done; bulk actions handle multiple at once.

text: Personal reminders keep individual follow-ups inside the workspace rather than scattered across sticky notes or a separate to-do app, and surfacing due-dates on the calendar means personal commitments and scheduled meetings live on one timeline.

**Frontend:** `RemindersView.tsx` (`mode==='reminders'`), Rail count badge. **Backend:** `routes/reminders.ts` — folders + reminders CRUD + `/bulk`; `services/reminderService.ts`. **DB:** `reminders` (`text`, `done`, `due_at`, `priority`, `status`, `recurrence`, `folder_id`; migration 0014) and `folders`. **Realtime:** `REMINDER_CHANGED` to the owner's user room → client refetch.

items: Authentication/Users (owner-scoped).
Calendar (due-date overlay).
Realtime plane (owner-scoped change signal).

text: Files is the document store and sharing surface: upload, browse, favorite, share with users/conversations, generate public download links, and download — all auth-gated and served same-origin. It is shipped, backed by S3-compatible object storage (MinIO) with an automatic MySQL-BLOB fallback.

items: User opens Files (or attaches a file in a chat — same underlying store).
They upload; a progress bar tracks the XHR upload.
They favorite, share to a person or conversation at view/comment/edit permission, or create a public link.
They download; the file streams back through the same origin.

text: Keeping documents in the same governed system as conversations means access follows membership and explicit shares — no separate file-server permissions to manage — while same-origin delivery fixed cross-host 'couldn't load' attachment failures. The object-store-with-DB-fallback design keeps uploads working even if MinIO is temporarily unavailable.

**Frontend:** `FilesView.tsx` (`mode==='files'`); uploads use XHR for progress (`lib/api.ts uploadFile`). **Backend:** `routes/files.ts` — `GET /link/:token` (PUBLIC, registered *before* auth — the opaque token is the credential), then auth-gated `GET /`, `POST /` (upload, `express.raw` 100 MB, rate-limited 60/min before buffering), `GET /:id/download|presigned|details|shares`, `POST /:id/star|share|link`, deletes. `services/fileService.ts` resolves an effective permission (owner > edit > comment > view) from uploader, direct shares, share-link, or conversation membership; `storageService.ts` wraps S3 (`@aws-sdk/client-s3`, path-style). **DB:** `files` (`data` LONGBLOB now nullable, `storage_key` for S3, `share_token`, `link_permission`, `starred`); `file_shares`. **Delivery:** clients never talk to MinIO directly — download streams S3 → backend → Next proxy → browser (the same-origin model). Presigned URLs exist but are effectively unused for delivery because they point at the internal MinIO endpoint.

title: Honest limitations
text: On S3 failure the upload *silently* falls back to storing bytes in the MySQL `data` LONGBLOB (empty catch) — if MinIO is down, files quietly land in the DB with no operator alert. Default MinIO root credentials are weak and unenforced. There is no encryption-at-rest unless app-level E2EE is enabled (off by default), and the internal backend→MinIO hop is plain HTTP. Avatars/wallpapers are a *separate* path: compact downscaled JPEG data-URLs stored directly in the DB, not MinIO.

items: MinIO/S3 object storage (primary) + MySQL BLOB (fallback).
Conversations/Members (membership grants view access).
Messaging/Attachments (per-message files reference this store).
Recordings reuse the same storage service and bucket scheme.

text: Notifications is the backend subsystem that powers the Activity feed (2.8). It is shipped, in-app only (no web-push). It is documented here as a distinct subsystem because several modules *produce* notifications even though users *consume* them through Activity.

There is no separate user-facing surface beyond the Activity feed and the Rail badge — see 2.8 for the consumer flow. From a *producer* standpoint: when a user is @-mentioned, replied to, reacted to, called and missed, invited to a meeting, or has a file shared with them, a notification row is created and pushed.

Centralizing notification production in one service means every module raises notifications consistently (same types, same delivery, same read-state semantics) and the unread count is authoritative across modules.

**Backend:** `routes/notifications.ts` + `services/notificationService.ts` (`notifyMentions`, `notifyReply`, `notifyReaction`, `notifyCallMissed`, `notifyMeetingInvite`). **DB:** `notifications` (migration 0028). **Realtime:** producers emit `NOTIFICATION_NEW` to the recipient's user room and `NOTIFICATION_COUNT` to refresh the badge; reads emit `NOTIFICATION_READ`. The unread count is pushed live, so the badge updates without polling.

items: Messaging, Calls, Meetings, Files (producers).
Activity (the consumer surface).
Realtime plane (push).

text: Search lets users find messages across conversations using MySQL FULLTEXT indexing. **Status: PARTIAL — built but hidden by default.** The component, route, service, and index all exist and work; the nav entry is gated off behind the `globalSearch` feature flag and hidden in the Rail by default. Reactivation is a single env-var flip (`NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_GLOBAL_SEARCH=1`).

items: (When enabled) the user opens Search from the Rail and enters a query.
`SearchView.tsx` shows matching messages; clicking a result jumps to it in context.
With the flag off, the Search nav item simply does not appear — but the code path is intact.

text: Full-text search is what makes a long-lived message archive useful — finding a decision or file from weeks ago without scrolling. It is feature-flagged off in the current deployments (likely pending relevance/scale tuning), but the infrastructure is in place to enable instantly.

**Frontend:** `SearchView.tsx` (`mode==='search'`); `Rail.tsx` adds `search` to `HIDDEN_NAV` unless `config.features.globalSearch` is on. **Backend:** `routes/search.ts` (`GET /?q=`) + `services/searchService.ts`. **DB:** messages use the FULLTEXT index `idx_messages_fts` (migration 0017, InnoDB, boolean-mode prefix search, min token 3 chars).

title: Hidden, not absent
text: Search is fully implemented. Treat it as a dark-launched feature: the component, REST route, service, and DB index are production code; only the nav surface is gated. Flipping `NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_GLOBAL_SEARCH=1` re-exposes it with no other change.

items: Messaging (`messages` table + FTS index).
Feature-flag config (`globalSearch`).

text: Settings is the control surface for personalization and account behavior: theme, accent, density, zoom, font, font size, accessibility toggles, profile fields, manual presence, and receipt privacy. It is shipped. It is opened from the Rail footer (it is *not* a nav `mode`).

items: User opens Settings from the Rail footer.
They pick a theme (light/dark/oled/midnight/slate/forest/auto), accent, density, zoom, and font; toggle accessibility options (high-contrast, reduce-motion, larger-text, dyslexia-font, etc.).
They edit profile fields and set manual presence (auto/away/busy).
Changes apply live via `applySettings()` (body-class toggles) and persist to the backend.

text: Deep personalization and accessibility support broaden adoption (users with visual/motor needs, OLED power saving, large-display scaling) and let the product feel native to each user — reducing friction and support load while signaling enterprise polish.

**Frontend:** `Settings.tsx` (~1,822 lines) + `Onboarding.tsx`. `applySettings()` in `CoLabV1.tsx` toggles `body` classes (`font-<family>`, `accent-<name>`, density, theme classes) and sets `document.body.style.zoom`. **Backend:** `routes/settings.ts` + `services/settingsService.ts`. **DB:** `user_settings` is a per-user JSON blob (PK `user_id`, 1:1 with `users`). **Realtime:** a manual-presence change emits `USER_UPDATED` globally.

title: Settings whitelist gotcha
text: A frontend-only setting that is *not* present in the backend `DEFAULTS` is silently dropped on save. This caused the 'wallpaper not implemented' bug. When adding a new setting, you must add it to both the frontend control *and* the backend defaults whitelist, or it will never persist.

items: Authentication/Users (profile fields).
Presence/Status (manual presence lives here).
The theme/design system in `styles/v1.css` (consumes the toggled classes).

text: Presence shows whether a user is online — the green/idle dots on avatars. It is shipped, realtime-driven, with no dedicated route (it is a property of the socket connection).

Presence is passive from the user's perspective: connecting brings them online, disconnecting (tab close / network loss) brings them offline, and peers see the dot update in near-real-time on avatars in `ConversationSidebar` and elsewhere.
Knowing who is available right now is essential for synchronous collaboration — it tells a user whether to call, message, or wait, and it makes the workspace feel live rather than static.

**Backend:** `realtime/socket.ts` sets `db.users.setPresence(uid,'on')` on connect and `'off'` on disconnect, emitting `PRESENCE_UPDATE`. Fan-out is *scoped*: it goes only to conversation peers' user rooms (via `listPeerIds`), not a global `io.emit`, to avoid an O(N²) reconnect storm. **DB:** `users.presence` (default `off`) plus `last_seen` and `share_last_seen` privacy mirror (migration 0037). **Frontend:** presence dots in `Avatar.tsx` / `ConversationSidebar` react to the socket event.

title: Why scoped fan-out matters
text: If presence were broadcast globally, every reconnect in a large workspace would notify everyone — an N² storm on flaky networks. Scoping to actual conversation peers keeps presence cheap and multi-instance-safe across the Redis adapter.

items: Realtime plane (the entire mechanism).
`users` table (`presence`, `last_seen`).
Status (manual override sits on top of presence).

text: Status is the *manual* presence override on top of automatic presence: a user can force Away or Busy/DND regardless of their connection state. **Status: PARTIAL.** Only manual away/busy/DND exists — there is **no** free-text or emoji custom status (no `status_text`/`statusEmoji` columns or code).

items: User opens Settings and sets manual presence to `auto`, `away`, or `busy` (DND).
With `auto`, presence follows the socket connection; with a manual value, that value overrides until changed back.
Peers see the chosen state on the user's avatar/chip.

text: Manual status lets users signal availability intent — 'I'm online but heads-down' (DND) or 'stepping away' — which automatic presence cannot infer. It reduces unwanted interruptions during focus time.

**Backend:** `services/settingsService.ts` holds `manualPresence` ('auto'|'away'|'busy', DND serialized as 'busy'), mirrored onto `users.manual_presence` (migration 0039; NULL = fall back to auto) by the settings route, which then emits `USER_UPDATED` globally. **Frontend:** the control is in `Settings.tsx` (~line 1608).

title: Not built: custom status text/emoji
text: There is deliberately no rich custom-status feature — no 'In a meeting 🗓️' free-text/emoji. Only the three manual presence values exist. Do not represent custom status as a current capability; it would require new columns and UI.

items: Settings (the control surface).
Presence (the auto baseline it overrides).
Realtime plane (`USER_UPDATED` propagation).

text: Reactions let users respond to a message with an emoji, including a searchable emoji catalog and a who-reacted view. It is shipped (backend live-verified). Reactions are stored *inline* on the message, not in a separate table.

items: User hovers/opens a message's reaction bar and picks an emoji (searchable via the emoji catalog).
The reaction appears on the message for everyone; tapping it again toggles it off.
Tapping a reaction count reveals who reacted.

text: Lightweight acknowledgement (👍, ✅) reduces low-value 'ok' messages and gives quick group sentiment, keeping channels readable while still confirming receipt — a small feature with outsized impact on signal-to-noise.

**Frontend:** emoji picker via `lib/emojiData.ts` in `ChatView`; who-reacted UI. **Backend:** `services/messageService.ts toggleReaction`; socket path (`MESSAGE_REACT`) plus REST fallback `POST /api/conversations/:id/messages/:mid/react`. **DB:** stored in `messages.reactions_json` (inline JSON — no reactions table). **Realtime:** the update broadcasts as `MESSAGE_UPDATED` to the conversation room, and `notifyReaction` raises a `NOTIFICATION_NEW` to the message owner (if not self).

items: Messaging (reactions attach to messages).
Notifications (reaction notifies the owner).
`emojiData.ts` catalog.

text: Attachments are files sent inside a message (images, documents, etc.). It is shipped. Attachments are stored per-message as `file_json` and physically persisted via the Files module's storage — so they are a thin integration layer over Files, not a separate store.

items: User attaches a file in the composer; an XHR upload shows progress.
The message sends with the attachment; recipients see a preview/download chip.
Clicking downloads the file through the same-origin proxy.

text: Sharing a file in the flow of conversation (rather than uploading separately and pasting a link) is faster and keeps the file tied to its context. Same-origin delivery resolved the cross-host attachment-load failures that previously broke this in multi-host deployments.

**Frontend:** upload via `lib/api.ts uploadFile` (XHR progress) in `ChatView`. **Backend:** the upload hits `routes/files.ts` (`express.raw` 100 MB), and the resulting file reference is embedded in the message's `file_json`. **DB:** the bytes live in the `files` table (S3 `storage_key` or BLOB fallback); the message row carries the `file_json` pointer. **Delivery:** download streams S3 → backend → Next proxy → browser, same origin.

items: Files module + storage service (physical persistence).
Messaging (`file_json` on the message).
Same-origin Next proxy (delivery).

text: Channels are topic/team conversation spaces. It is shipped. A channel is a `conversations` row with `kind='channel'` — it shares the *entire* messaging stack with groups and DMs; there is no separate channel route or table.
A user opens or joins a channel from the sidebar and participates exactly as in any conversation — post, react, thread, pin, search — with the same UI as groups and DMs.

Channels organize broad, persistent, topic-based discussion (announcements, a project, a team) distinct from private DMs — the standard way teams structure communication at scale — while costing zero additional backend surface because they reuse the conversation primitive.

**Differentiated only by `kind`:** `conversations.kind='channel'` (constant in `shared/src/constants.ts`). All behavior comes from `conversationService.ts`, `ChatView.tsx`, and `ConversationSidebar.tsx` — the same `conversations`, `conversation_members`, and `messages` tables as groups and DMs. There is no channel-specific endpoint.

items: Messaging (entire stack).
Conversations/Members tables.
Reactions, Attachments, Search — inherited.

text: Groups are multi-person private conversations with managed membership and group calls. It is shipped. A group is `conversations.kind='group'`, sharing the messaging stack; it adds member management and group-call/host controls.

items: User creates a group (via the create-group modal) and adds members.
The group behaves as any conversation for messaging; an admin can add/remove participants and manage the group.
A member can start a group call (huddle); owner/admin can mute-all or remove a participant in-call.

text: Groups support small-team and ad-hoc collaboration with controlled membership — the right granularity between a 1:1 DM and an open channel — and the group-call host controls keep multi-party calls orderly.

**Frontend:** group management modals are exported from `Modals.tsx` (CreateGroup/ManageGroup/AddParticipants). **Backend:** `conversationService.ts` handles member add/remove (excluding dm/self); group-call host controls live in `routes/calls.ts` (`/group/:convId/controls/...`, owner/admin-gated). **DB:** same `conversations`/`conversation_members`/`messages` tables, `kind='group'`. **Realtime:** member changes and system messages (add/leave) broadcast as conversation events and `MESSAGE_NEW` system pills.

items: Messaging stack and Conversations/Members.
Calls (group huddle + host controls).
`Modals.tsx` management surfaces.

text: Direct Messages are private 1:1 conversations (plus a 'self' self-DM). It is shipped. A DM is `conversations.kind='dm'`, with a uniqueness guarantee (one DM per pair) and optional end-to-end encryption (off by default).

items: User starts a DM from a contact or by accepting a connection request (DMs are gated by an accepted invite/connection).
They converse 1:1 with the full messaging feature set.
If E2EE is enabled in the deployment, DM content is encrypted client-side; otherwise it is plaintext like other conversations.

text: Private 1:1 conversation is the most basic and most-used collaboration primitive; the connection-gate (you can't DM an arbitrary stranger until a connection is accepted) reduces spam, and optional E2EE offers a server-blind privacy tier for sensitive conversations without affecting the rest of the product.

**DB uniqueness:** `conversations.dm_key` (deterministic sorted member-pair key) with a unique index (migrations 0034/0035) enforces one DM per pair. **Gating:** DM creation/send is gated by an accepted connection (`invites`) and blocked-user enforcement (`user_blocks`). **E2EE (optional, DM-only):** `routes/e2ee.ts` + `lib/e2ee/*` implement native Web Crypto ECIES (P-256 ECDH + HKDF + AES-GCM, per-recipient-device sealing). The server stores only public keys and opaque ciphertext — a DB dump cannot read DM content. It is OFF by default on both sides (`NEXT_PUBLIC_E2EE_ENABLED` / `E2EE_ENABLED`) and *fail-closed* when on. Everything else uses the standard messaging stack.

title: E2EE — do not overclaim
text: DM E2EE is custom native-WebCrypto ECIES, NOT the Signal protocol. There is no forward secrecy yet (per-message ephemerals give confidentiality vs the server but not against device-key theft), and the safety-number computation exists but is not wired into any UI. It is DM/self-conversation only — groups, channels, calls, and meetings are never E2EE.

items: Messaging stack and Conversations.
Invites/Connections (DM gate) and Blocks.
Optional E2EE library + `routes/e2ee.ts` + e2ee tables (dormant when off).

text: Voice messages let users record and send short audio clips in a conversation; separately, voicemails let an unanswered call leave audio for the recipient. Both are shipped. (Slide-to-cancel recording UX is deferred per project notes.)

items: In a chat, the user records a voice note and sends it; recipients play it inline via `VoicePlayer.tsx`.
On an unanswered call, the caller can leave a voicemail; the recipient sees and plays it from their voicemail list.

text: Voice is faster than typing for nuanced or lengthy thoughts and conveys tone; voicemail ensures a missed call still delivers its message. Both reduce back-and-forth and missed-context, especially for distributed or mobile users.

**Voice messages:** `VoicePlayer.tsx` + record UI in `ChatView`; the message carries a `voice` field and `type='voice'` (migration 0023), routed through `messageService.ts`. **Voicemail:** `services/voicemailService.ts` + `routes/calls.ts` voicemail endpoints (`POST /voicemail` uses `express.raw`); the audio is stored in the `files` table and the row lives in the `voicemails` table (migration 0016), owned by the recipient.

items: Messaging (voice message path) / Calls (voicemail path).
Files/storage (audio bytes).
`voicemails` table.

text: Screen sharing lets a participant publish their screen (with best-effort tab/system audio) in both 1:1/group calls and meetings. It is shipped, using identical LiveKit code in both paths.

items: In a call or meeting, the user clicks Share Screen and picks a window/tab/display.
The screen publishes as a track; others see it as a tile.
Clicking Stop ends the share; if the user cancels the picker, nothing changes.

text: Screen sharing is essential for demos, walkthroughs, pair work, and presentations — it turns a call into a working session and removes the need to describe what's on screen. Including best-effort system audio means shared videos/demos carry their sound.

**Both paths, identical call:** `localParticipant.setScreenShareEnabled(next, { audio:true, systemAudio:'include' })`. In meetings it lives in `MeetingStage.tsx toggleScreen` (~line 1068, reverts `screen` state on throw); in 1:1/group calls it lives in `CoLabV1.tsx toggleScreen` (~line 7720, swallows a throw = user cancelled the picker). It is LiveKit-based with no separate route or table. If the browser/user declines audio, the video share still publishes.

items: Calls and Meetings (the two host contexts).
LiveKit SFU (media).

text: Recording captures a meeting to a stored file for later playback. **Status: PARTIAL.** The backend is fully implemented (service, table, routes) and there are *two* recording paths, but server-side egress is not enabled in current deployments because it depends on the egress worker container.

items: A host starts recording in a meeting.
Path A (server-side egress): LiveKit Egress records and uploads the MP4 — but if egress is not provisioned, the endpoint returns an honest 503.
Path B (client-side): a browser `MediaRecorder` captures and uploads webm/mp4 to storage — this works without egress.
Recordings are listed and played back via the auth-gated, membership-checked download stream.

text: Recordings let absent colleagues catch up, preserve decisions, and support compliance/training. The dual-path design means basic recording (client-side) works even where the heavier egress infrastructure isn't deployed — graceful degradation rather than a hard dependency.

**Backend:** `services/recordingService.ts` + recording endpoints in `routes/meetings.ts` (start/stop, upload via `express.raw` 300 MB, streamed download). **Egress path:** LiveKit Egress uploads MP4 via the SDK to the same S3/MinIO config; finalization is confirmed by the LiveKit webhook (`routes/livekit.ts`, signature-verified, raw body). **DB:** `meeting_recordings` (status, `storage_key`, `playback_url`, `egress_id`, duration, size; migration 0015). Playback is never a public/presigned URL — always the membership-checked download stream.

title: Honest status: code done, egress not provisioned
text: All recording *code* ships. Server-side egress requires the egress worker container and `EGRESS_ENABLED`; without it, the egress start endpoint returns 503 by design. Client-side `MediaRecorder` recording works without egress. Do not represent server-side meeting recording as 'live' in a deployment until the egress container is confirmed running.

items: Meetings (the only context).
LiveKit Egress (server-side path) + egress container.
Files/storage service + `meeting_recordings` table.
LiveKit webhook route (egress finalization).

text: AI features bring an OpenAI-compatible assistant into the workspace — conversation summarization ('Catch up') and a general ask endpoint. **Status: PARTIAL.** The backend (`routes/ai.ts` + `aiService.ts`, branded 'Agen-X') is implemented, but only *summarize* is surfaced in the UI (and gated off by default); the *ask* endpoint exists with **no UI calling it**. The real, working AI lives in `aiService.ts` — NOT in the `agents/` scaffold (see 2.26).

items: (When `aiSummary` is enabled) the user clicks 'Catch up' in a conversation; the assistant summarizes the recent messages.
The general ask assistant has no UI — `api.askAgent` is defined but called from nowhere.
If the LLM is not configured, the endpoints return `AI_DISABLED` (503) and make no outbound calls.

text: Conversation summarization saves time catching up on a busy thread — the highest-value, lowest-risk AI use case. Keeping it behind a flag and behind explicit LLM configuration means the product ships zero AI cost/risk by default and can enable it deliberately, with E2EE-encrypted messages excluded from summaries to preserve privacy guarantees.

**Backend:** `routes/ai.ts` — `POST /summarize`, `POST /ask` (both auth-gated). `services/aiService.ts` calls an OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions`; `summarizeConversation` enforces conversation membership (no IDOR), skips E2EE rows, and pulls the last ~60 messages. AI is gated in config: `enabled = LLM_BASE_URL!==''` — when unset, it reports `AI_DISABLED`. **Frontend:** only `api.summarizeConversation` is wired (`ChatView.tsx` ~line 4037), gated by `config.features.aiSummary`. `api.askAgent` exists (`lib/api.ts` ~line 616) but is never invoked by any component.

title: Honest status
text: AI is doubly gated: it needs an LLM configured AND the `aiSummary` flag on, and even then only summarization has UI. The 'ask' assistant is an endpoint with no front door. Treat AI as a partial, opt-in capability, not a headline feature.

items: An external OpenAI-compatible LLM (`LLM_BASE_URL`).
Messaging (summaries read messages, skip E2EE rows).
Feature-flag config (`aiSummary`).
NOT the `agents/` module — that is a separate scaffold.

text: Agents is intended to be an AI Workspace Companion (daily briefings, conversation summaries, workspace insights). **Status: ABSENT as a functioning feature.** The `agents/` workspace is an explicit scaffold — every method throws `not implemented (Sprint 6)` — and the in-app `AgentsView.tsx` is a static governance/marketing page. The nav item is hidden by default.

There is no functional user flow. With the `agents` flag off, the nav item is hidden; if shown, `AgentsView.tsx` displays an informational governance page ('No agents connected', 'MCP not configured') — it does not run anything.

The intended value (proactive briefings and insights that reduce manual triage) is real but not yet delivered. Today the module's value is architectural: it reserves a clean namespace and a governance narrative ('an agent never gets direct database or network access') for a future sprint, and the `AgentsView` page communicates that governance posture.

**Frontend:** `AgentsView.tsx` is a static page; nav gated by `config.features.agents` (in `Rail.tsx HIDDEN_NAV`). **Backend:** none — there is no agent route, table, runtime, planner, model wiring, or memory. `agents/app/src/index.ts` exports a single `companion` object whose `dailyBriefing`/`summarizeConversation`/`workspaceInsights` methods all throw. It is imported by no consumer; it participates only in the lint/build graph.

title: Do not represent Agents as a feature
text: Agents is an interface-only stub for a future 'Sprint 6'. There is no agent loop, no LLM call, no memory, and no code path connecting an agent to the MCP server. The working summarization capability is the separate AI Features module (2.25), which coincidentally shares a method name. Treat `agents/` as a reserved namespace, not a functioning system.

items: None functional. (Conceptually would consume AI Features + MCP in a future sprint.)

text: MCP is a server that exposes CoLab's capabilities as tools/resources/prompts for AI agents, proxied through the REST backend. **Status: PARTIAL — built but standalone and unwired.** A real implementation exists (gateway, 20 tools, 7 resources, 1 prompt, two transports), but it is a hand-rolled JSON-RPC scaffold, not run in any deployment, and nothing in the app invokes it.

There is no in-app user flow. An external MCP client could (in principle) connect to the stdio or SSE transport to list/call tools, but `AgentsView` states 'No MCP server is configured in this deployment', and no compose file runs it.

The intended value is a governed automation surface — letting AI agents act in the workspace (send messages, schedule meetings, create tasks) *only* through audited REST endpoints, never direct DB/network access. That governance model is the architectural payoff; the runtime value is not yet realized because the server isn't deployed or wired.

**Code:** `mcp/app/src` — `server/gateway.ts` (BackendGateway proxies GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE to the backend with a Bearer token + optional `X-CoLab-Tenant`), `tools/index.ts` (20 tools: send_message, schedule_message, create_meeting, create_task, etc.), `resources/index.ts` (7 resources), `prompts/index.ts` (1 prompt), and two transports: stdio (line-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0, partial — no `initialize` handshake) and SSE (discovery-only — it *cannot* invoke tools). **Auth:** the gateway requires a token or throws; backend responses must be `{ok:true,data}` or it throws. **Not the official SDK** (no `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`), no build step, no start script, not containerized as a service.

title: Honest status
text: MCP is real code but standalone. It proxies the live REST API, but no deployment runs it and no frontend/backend path calls it. The SSE transport is discovery-only; the stdio transport is not spec-complete (no initialize/notifications/batching). Treat it as a prototype integration surface, not a live capability.

items: The CoLab REST backend (every tool/resource proxies to it).
A bearer token (governance: no direct DB/network access).
Not wired to Agents or any running service.

text: This matrix is the honest, at-a-glance status of every module covered above. 'Shipped' means in production use; 'Partial' means built but hidden, only partially surfaced, or dependent on un-provisioned infrastructure; 'Absent' means scaffold-only with no runtime behavior.

rows: Media plane needs TLS+TURN per deploy
View over meetings; no own table
Only summarize has UI; ask unwired
